title: Fatal startup errors are re-thrown with no logging, breaking incident detection
description: The application bootstrap in app.ts awaits dependency validation and server startup, and on any failure the top-level .catch handler simply re-throws the error (line 16) with no logging call of any kind. If validateDependencies() (line 8) detects a compromised or vulnerable dependency, or if server.start() (line 11) fails due to a misconfiguration, credential issue, or attack-related condition (e.g., port hijack, TLS cert problem), the only observable behavior is an uncaught exception that terminates the process. There is no structured log entry recording what failed, when, or why. In production this means: (1) operators cannot distinguish a security-relevant startup failure (e.g., dependency integrity check failing because of a supply-chain tampering) from a benign transient error, (2) there is no timestamp/correlation id captured for later incident reconstruction, and (3) repeated crash-restart loops caused by an attacker-triggered condition would generate no alertable signal. This is the sole error-handling path for the entire application's bootstrap, so its complete absence of logging is a genuine security logging/monitoring gap rather than a minor style issue.

await validateDependencies() can reject/throw if a security-relevant dependency check fails; the error propagates up through app()'s promise with no logging at this point.

The server module is dynamically imported; a failure here (e.g. module resolution or init error) would also flow to the same unlogged rejection path.

The single .catch clause treats all failures uniformly by re-throwing, with no differentiation, alerting, or safe-mode fallback for a failed security dependency check.

title: No graceful failure/alerting path for startup dependency validation — fail-crash design with no compensating control
description: The design of app.ts treats a dependency-validation failure or server-start failure identically to any other exception: it terminates the process via an uncaught throw (lines 14-17), with no retry logic, no alert hook, no fallback safe-mode, and no distinction between transient vs. security-critical failures (e.g., a validateDependencies() check that exists specifically to catch known-vulnerable or tampered dependencies, per its name). Because there is no compensating control (alert, paging hook, structured incident log) wired into this single choke point, a security-relevant startup failure (such as detection of a vulnerable/malicious dependency) produces the exact same silent crash as a trivial misconfiguration typo, meaning defenders have no way to prioritize or detect the security-relevant case out of band. This is a design gap: the file is the sole place where such failures are centrally handled, and the design never establishes a path for surfacing/alerting on security-relevant startup failures versus ordinary ones.

The result of the security check is awaited; any failure here is indistinguishable in downstream handling from any other kind of error.
The single .catch clause treats all failures uniformly by re-throwing, with no differentiation, alerting, or safe-mode fallback for a failed security dependency check.

title: Business-critical order and review data stored only in an in-memory, non-persistent database
description: reviewsCollection and ordersCollection are instantiated with `new MarsDB.Collection(...)` and no schema, validator, or allowed-operator whitelist is attached at creation time. Because MarsDB (like MongoDB) accepts arbitrary JavaScript objects as query/update documents, any downstream code that forwards user-controlled input directly into find()/update()/insert() calls on these collections (a common Juice Shop pattern, e.g. search or filter endpoints) can inject Mongo-style query operators (e.g. $where, $gt, $ne) unless the caller independently sanitizes input. The design here establishes no server-side re-validation boundary or schema constraint at the data-access layer itself — the collections are configured with defaults only, offloading all safety entirely to whatever code happens to call them. Compounding this, the module opts out of TypeScript's type checking for the whole MarsDB surface, so even the compiler cannot flag a caller passing an unexpected/attacker-shaped object into these collections. This is a missing security control at the point where the trust boundary should be enforced (the data layer), not merely a caller-side bug.

ordersCollection, holding financial/transactional order records, is likewise created purely in-memory and exported; any process restart or crash silently destroys all order history with no recovery path.

title: No audit logging wrapper around order/review data-layer operations
description: The data module that centralizes access to security-relevant business records (orders and reviews) exposes the raw MarsDB Collection objects directly with no interception, hooks, or logging wrapper for create/update/delete operations. Security-relevant events at this layer — order creation, order modification/cancellation, review creation/deletion — have no place in this file where they would be recorded (e.g., no event emitter, no audit-log call, no correlation-ID stamping). Since this is the sole module responsible for constructing these collections, and no logging control is established here or attached to the collection objects before export, any code that uses reviewsCollection/ordersCollection downstream has to independently implement its own audit logging or none will exist. This absence at the central data-access point makes it structurally likely that data-modifying operations on financial/order records go unlogged, hindering incident detection and forensic reconstruction of who changed which order or review and when.

title: NFT contract interface exposes single-step, unconfirmed ownership transfer/renouncement
description: The nftABI exported here defines the client-facing interface the frontend uses to call transferOwnership(address newOwner) and renounceOwnership() on the deployed NFT contract. Both are irreversible, privilege-critical operations exposed as single-call functions with no two-step handoff (no pendingOwner/acceptOwnership pattern) and no confirmation step visible in the interface. Because this file is the contract of record the application code will use to build these calls, any UI or script built against it can transfer or permanently renounce contract ownership in one transaction with no compensating control (e.g., a typo'd address in transferOwnership immediately and irrecoverably hands control to an unintended party; renounceOwnership immediately and irrecoverably strips the contract of an owner). This is the classic 'irreversible action without confirmation/compensating control' design gap called out for inherently risky operations. The defect is in the interface design being relied upon (single-step admin transfer) rather than in a missing validation of one field.

The function name/output confirm ownership is reassigned in a single call; consumers of this exported ABI (elsewhere in the app) will build a one-shot transaction against this signature.

title: Wallet contract interface permits crediting balances to arbitrary addresses via payable deposit, decoupled from withdrawal authorization
description: web3WalletABI exposes ethdeposit(address _to) as a payable function that lets any caller send ETH while nominating an arbitrary '_to' address to be credited (see balances/userWithdrawing view functions keyed by address), and a separate withdraw(uint256 _amount) that presumably withdraws against the caller's own tracked balance. Decoupling 'who pays' from 'whose balance is credited' is a known anti-pattern that enables forced-deposit/griefing style manipulation of another user's on-chain accounting exposed through this app's Web3 integration, and the presence of a ContractExploited event in the same ABI indicates the integrated contract itself anticipates being exploited. Because this file is the canonical interface the application uses to interact with the wallet contract, any code built on it inherits this trust assumption (the server/client never re-derives or restricts which address may be credited) without validating the safety of allowing arbitrary third-party crediting before exposing it to end users.

balances(address) and userWithdrawing(address) are per-address accounting views keyed by the arbitrary address suppliable via ethdeposit, meaning any caller can influence another address's tracked balance/withdrawing state.
name: '_to' — the destination address whose balance is credited is caller-controlled and independent of whoever actually sends the ETH.

withdraw(uint256 _amount) takes only an amount with no address parameter, implying it operates against the caller's own balances/userWithdrawing entry — the same entry that a third party could have influenced via a prior ethdeposit call naming the caller as '_to'.

The ABI declares a ContractExploited(address culprit) event, indicating the underlying contract this interface targets has a known exploit condition that the application nonetheless integrates with via this exported ABI without any documented compensating control in the interface.

title: Sensitive account-recovery secrets modeled as exportable/importable backup data
description: The Backup interface treats continueCode, continueCodeFindIt and continueCodeFixIt — server-issued secrets used by Juice Shop's password-recovery / two-step verification flows to authenticate a user without a password — as ordinary optional fields of a generic 'Backup' data object, on par with UI preference fields like language and banner status. The architecture shows a POST /file-upload route wired to handleYamlUpload, which is the well-known Juice Shop backup-restore feature that parses a user-supplied YAML file into this Backup shape and applies it to the account. Because the model does not distinguish security-critical continuation codes from cosmetic settings, and because this shape is what a client-supplied backup file is deserialized into, the design permits a user-controlled file to carry values for continueCode/continueCodeFindIt/continueCodeFixIt end-to-end into the restore path. If the (unseen) restore handler applies these fields from the uploaded object rather than re-deriving them server-side, an attacker who can access another user's backup (or forge one) could read or overwrite the codes that gate account recovery — a trust-boundary violation where a client-editable structure carries fields the server alone should ever set. The interface is declared as a single contiguous block (lines 6-13); every field in that block, including the non-sensitive version/language/banners fields, is exported with equal, unmarked mutability, so nothing in the type itself prevents a deserializer from populating the sensitive continuation codes alongside the cosmetic ones.

continueCodeFindIt, an account-recovery secret for the 'find it' challenge track, likewise modeled as freely settable backup data.

Closing brace completes and exports the Backup type; this fully-assembled, undifferentiated shape is what any restore/import routine (outside this file) will type-check untrusted deserialized backup data against, allowing attacker-controlled continueCode* values to flow through unguarded.

continueCodeFixIt included as another restorable field; the model provides no server-only/immutable marker, so any consumer that maps client-supplied backup data onto this interface can carry attacker-controlled values into these security-critical fields.

title: Global mutable singleton used to pass blueprint file path across requests (race condition / cross-user info disclosure)
description: The module keeps a single, process-wide `let retrieveBlueprintChallengeFile` variable (line 33) that is written by an exported setter (line 34-36) and presumably read elsewhere to serve a file to whichever request asks for it. Because Node.js modules are singletons, this value is shared by every concurrent request/user rather than being scoped to a session or request. The design never establishes any binding between the value that was set and the specific user/session that is entitled to read it back. An attacker can race a legitimate user's upload/retrieve flow: while User A triggers the code path that calls setRetrieveBlueprintChallengeFile with their file path, User B (or the attacker) can trigger the corresponding read path and receive User A's file path/content instead of their own, or overwrite the value before User A's read completes causing User A to retrieve the attacker's file. This is a design flaw — even a perfectly implemented setter/getter pair built on this global variable cannot prevent cross-user interference, because the architecture itself has no per-request isolation.

Value is stored in a single module-level `let` variable shared across all concurrent requests for the entire process lifetime.

Assignment overwrites the previous value; any other module reading the exported `retrieveBlueprintChallengeFile` binding afterwards receives whichever value was written last, regardless of which user/session it belongs to, enabling a race condition and cross-user information disclosure.

title: Unencapsulated, ownership-agnostic in-memory data stores enabling IDOR-style design gaps
description: users, products, feedback, baskets, basketItems and complaints (lines 15-20) are exported as plain mutable `Record<string, T>` objects with no accessor functions, no ownership checks, and no invariant enforcement (e.g. uniqueness, foreign-key consistency, or 'this basket belongs to this user'). Any importing module can read or write any entry directly by key. According to the routing context, `PUT /api/BasketItems/:id` and `POST /api/BasketItems` are protected only by `security.appendUserId()`, which merely stamps the caller's user id onto the request — it does not consult this data layer to verify that the basket/basketItem referenced by `:id` actually belongs to the requesting user. Because the data-store design never requires or exposes an ownership-checked accessor (e.g., `getBasketItemForUser(id, userId)`), the correctness of access control is left entirely to whichever caller remembers to check it, and every one of the six stores in this file is declared the same unencapsulated way, so the gap is systemic rather than a one-off oversight in a single store. Any caller (present or future) that indexes `basketItems[id]` directly bypasses ownership enforcement entirely. This is a design gap: the store never establishes 'a value the server must decide rather than accept from the caller,' i.e., basket/item ownership, as an enforced invariant at the persistence layer.

title: No audit trail for mutations to security-relevant in-memory stores
description: The central application data stores (users, products, baskets, basketItems, complaints, challenges, feedback) are mutated directly by external callers with no logging hook anywhere in this module. Security-relevant events that would flow through this layer — user record creation/modification, complaint submission, basket/basket-item changes tied to purchases — are never recorded here, and since this is the single choke point for all in-memory persistence, there is no alternate place in this file where such an audit trail could be added incidentally. Every store in the file (lines 15-20) is declared and exposed the same bare way, so the absence of logging is uniform across the whole persistence layer, not limited to one record type. This absence prevents reconstruction of who changed what, when — e.g., detecting a user record being tampered with, or repeated anomalous basket manipulation attempts — since no correlation id, timestamp, or actor is captured at the point of mutation.

baskets store is likewise mutated directly by callers with no intervening logging call in this module.
products store is likewise mutated directly by callers with no logging hook in this module, showing the pattern is consistent across record types.
feedback store, which can carry user-submitted content, is exposed the same way with no mutation event captured.

complaints store is written to directly with no logging of the mutation event (actor, timestamp, previous/new value), leaving no audit trail for later incident investigation.

title: Unsanitized file parameter enables path traversal / arbitrary local file read in loadStaticData
description: The exported function loadStaticData(file: string) builds a filesystem path by directly concatenating the caller-supplied `file` argument into a path string (`'./data/static/' + file + '.yml'`) and then resolves and reads it with no validation, allow-listing, or sanitization of `file`. If any caller elsewhere in the application passes externally influenced input to this function (it is exported and generically named, taking any string), an attacker who controls `file` can inject path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../somewhere/target`) to make the resolved path escape the intended `./data/static/` directory and read arbitrary `.yml` files elsewhere on disk that the process can access. The `.yml` suffix constrains but does not eliminate exploitability against any reachable YAML file. Because the caller of this exported function is not visible in this file, reachability with attacker input cannot be fully confirmed here, but the function itself performs no defensive check between receiving `file` and using it to construct/read a filesystem path.

`file` is concatenated directly into a filesystem path string and passed to path.resolve with no character allow-listing or traversal-sequence check.
readFile(filePath, 'utf8') reads whatever file the resolved (potentially traversed) path points to.

title: Tainted file path written to log without sanitization (log injection)
description: On a read failure, the same unsanitized, caller-controlled path string that was built from the `file` parameter is written directly into a log message via logger.error. If `file` can contain control characters (e.g. CR/LF) or other injectable content, an attacker able to influence the `file` argument could forge or split log entries, undermining log integrity and making log-based detection/investigation unreliable. The tainted `filePath` value is captured by closure across the whole read/parse promise chain (the readFile call and the chained .then(safeLoad)) before reaching the .catch handler that performs the logging, so the value passes unmodified through the entire chain to the sink.

title: YAML content parsed without size/complexity limits (potential resource exhaustion)
description: loadStaticData reads whatever file the (possibly traversal-influenced) path resolves to and immediately parses its full contents with js-yaml's safeLoad, with no size cap, depth limit, or anchor/alias expansion restriction. YAML's alias/anchor expansion feature ('billion laughs'-style payloads) can cause exponential memory/CPU blow-up during parsing regardless of the 'safe' schema being used (safeLoad restricts which object types can be constructed, it does not limit reference expansion). If the file being loaded can be influenced or substituted by an attacker (e.g. via the path traversal weakness in loadStaticData, or if any static YAML file under the served directory can be attacker-modified/uploaded elsewhere in the app), parsing it here would consume excessive server resources with a single request, causing denial of service.

Full file contents are read into memory with no size limit before parsing.
The selector is concatenated into filePath and resolved, determining which file's full contents will be read and parsed next with no restriction on its size or structure.
safeLoad(...) parses the entire YAML content with no depth/size/alias-expansion guard, exposing the call to YAML entity-expansion denial-of-service if the parsed content is attacker-influenced.

title: No sanitized/public DTO types — internal persistence models re-exported directly as API-facing types
description: This file defines the application's canonical `User`, `Card`, `SecurityAnswer`, `Memory`, `Basket`, etc. types as bare aliases of their Sequelize/DB model types (e.g. `export type User = UserModel`, `export type Card = CardModel`, `export type SecurityAnswer = SecurityAnswerModel`). There is no separate 'public' or 'safe' view type that strips sensitive fields (password hash, TOTP secret, security question answers, full card numbers, internal timestamps, etc.) before data crosses the trust boundary to the client. Because route handlers elsewhere in the codebase are typed against these same aliases, the type system provides no compile-time signal that a handler must scrub sensitive fields before sending a `User`, `Card`, or `SecurityAnswer` object in an HTTP response — the design never establishes a distinction between 'what is stored' and 'what may be returned to a caller'. Walking the file top to bottom confirms the pattern is systemic and never broken: every model-backed type (`Delivery`, `Address`, `Card`, `Product`, the inline `Review` interface, `Recycle`, `SecurityQuestion`, `SecurityAnswer`, `Memory`) follows the same 1:1 alias with no masked counterpart anywhere in the file. This is a design-level trust violation: the server relies on individual handlers to remember to filter fields rather than the type contract enforcing it, which is exactly the kind of gap that leads to leaking password hashes, TOTP secrets, or full card data in API responses. The entrypoints that actually serialize these objects (e.g. GET /api/Users/:id, /rest/user routes) live outside this file, but the missing type-level control originates here.

The inline `Review` interface is hand-declared here (not a pure alias) yet still exposes `author` and `likedBy` fields with no redaction, showing the file never distinguishes internal vs. public shape even where it defines a type from scratch.

`BasketItem = BasketItemModel` further extends the unmasked-model surface within the checkout flow, with still no masked `Card` type introduced anywhere in the file.

`Memory` type likewise aliases the full `MemoryModel`; combined with the other aliases, no type in this file distinguishes stored/internal representation from what is safe to serialize to an untrusted client — handlers outside this file (not visible here) that return these types have no compile-time enforcement preventing sensitive-field leakage.

title: Card model type exposes full payment card representation with no masked/tokenized alternative type
description: `export type Card = CardModel` (line 23) makes the complete payment card model — which typically includes full card number, expiry, and cardholder name in Juice Shop's schema — the canonical type used across the codebase for representing a card, including presumably in list/detail API responses (e.g. GET card endpoints). There is no companion type in this file representing a masked card (e.g. last 4 digits only) for use in responses, which is the standard compensating control for handling stored payment data. Since this file is the single source of truth for the shape of 'Card' used throughout the app, the absence of a masked variant here means any consumer that needs to return card data to a client has to manually remember to redact fields, rather than being forced to do so by the type contract — an inherently risky operation (return of financial instrument data) with no built-in compensating control at the design level.

title: Cypress task exposes production coupon-minting logic with unvalidated discount value
description: The setupNodeEvents 'task' handler registers a GenerateCoupon task that takes a raw `discount: number` parameter from the caller and passes it directly into the real production security module (`security.generateCoupon(discount)`, imported from `./lib/insecurity` at line 2 — the same module presumably used to validate coupons at checkout). There is no bounds checking, type validation, or business-rule enforcement on `discount` before it reaches the coupon-minting function: nothing here prevents a caller of this task from requesting a coupon for 100% off, a negative discount that could invert into a credit, or any other out-of-range value. Because the task wires an external, uncontrolled input straight into a security-sensitive value-generation routine that produces artifacts trusted elsewhere in the application (redeemed coupons), the design never establishes a bound on what `discount` may be — the server-side re-derivation/validation step that should clamp or reject invalid discount values is absent from this call path. If this task interface is reachable by anything other than a fully trusted CI harness (e.g. a compromised e2e spec, a shared/misconfigured Cypress runner, or a supply-chain-compromised test dependency), an attacker gains a direct oracle to mint arbitrary-value coupons using the production secret/algorithm.

GenerateCoupon(discount: number) accepts an unvalidated numeric parameter with no range/type checks.

The identifier `security` used at the sink resolves to the module imported here (`./lib/insecurity`), binding the task directly to the production coupon-generation implementation rather than a test-only stub.

title: Unrestricted arbitrary configuration-key disclosure task
description: The GetFromConfig task takes an arbitrary string `variable` supplied by the caller and returns `config.get(variable)` verbatim, with no allow-list of permitted keys. Every other config-reading task in this file (GetOverwriteUrl, GetPastebinLeakProduct, GetBlueprint, GetChristmasProduct, GetTamperingProductId) is narrowly scoped to a single known, non-sensitive challenge-related key, but GetFromConfig removes that scoping entirely and turns the task into a generic config-value oracle. If the underlying `config` module (loaded from the `config` package, line 3) contains any secrets, credentials, internal URLs, or other sensitive settings anywhere in its tree (a common pattern for Node 'config' packages that hold DB connection strings, session secrets, or third-party API keys), this task will happily return them to whoever can invoke it. The design never establishes which configuration keys are safe to expose through this interface — it trusts the caller-supplied key name completely.

title: Client-side Product model exposes mutable price fields with no server-authority markers
description: The Product interface (and the ProductTableEntry type derived from it) models price-related fields (price, deluxePrice, points) as plain, freely mutable numbers with no readonly modifier and no indication in the type system that these values are server-authoritative and must be re-validated/re-derived server side. Because TypeScript interfaces have no runtime enforcement, any frontend code elsewhere in the Angular app (cart/basket components, checkout flows, order summary screens) that consumes this type can read, display, and re-transmit these fields to backend endpoints as part of order/basket update requests. If any such caller (not visible in this file) trusts the client-held price/deluxePrice value instead of having the server recompute it from the canonical product record, an attacker can tamper with the in-memory object (e.g., via browser devtools, a modified bundle, or intercepted/replayed API calls) to alter price before it is sent back, achieving a classic price-manipulation attack. This is a design gap in this file: it defines no distinction between server-owned fields (id, price, deluxePrice, points) and client-editable fields (quantity), so any consumer built against this type has no structural signal that these numeric fields must never be trusted verbatim from the client. The gap persists through the entire shape of the interface (every economic field between price and deluxePrice, including the optional points field) and is carried forward unchanged into the composite ProductTableEntry type used for cart/basket display and totals. This is reported as a low-to-medium confidence insecure-design finding because the actual sink (an endpoint or component that accepts this object and writes it to an order) is outside this file and not directly observable here.

title: Client-controlled 'unlocked' flag on Hint model enables trust-boundary bypass of hint-unlock business logic
description: The Hint interface exposes an optional boolean field `unlocked` alongside the hint's `id`, `ChallengeId`, `text`, and `order`. This model is the shape used by the Angular frontend to both receive hint data from the REST API and, presumably, to construct/submit Hint objects back to the server (the architecture summary lists POST /api/Hints and GET /api/Hints/:id as live REST endpoints backed by a generic Sequelize-style CRUD handler). Because `unlocked` is modeled as a plain, client-settable boolean property on the same object that is sent to create/update endpoints, the design does not establish any separation between data the client is allowed to set (text, order) and state the server must independently compute and enforce (whether a given hint has actually been earned/paid for by the player, e.g. via reputation points or failed-attempt count on the parent Challenge). All five fields of the interface (id, ChallengeId, text, order, unlocked) travel together as one object literal wherever this model is used, so any code path that serializes a Hint for a create/update request necessarily bundles the client-writable `unlocked` state alongside the other fields with no field-level distinction between 'client may set this' and 'server must derive this'. If the backend's generic CRUD handler for /api/Hints accepts and persists whatever body is posted (a common pattern for these auto-generated model REST routes), a user could submit or modify a Hint payload with `unlocked: true` (optionally paired with a chosen `ChallengeId` and `order`) to reveal a challenge hint they have not legitimately unlocked, or to reassign/reorder hints across challenges. Even if the current UI only reads this field, the interface itself provides no server-side re-derivation contract — the trust boundary that should force `unlocked` to be computed server-side is never established in this model, which is the root of the insecure design: the client is allowed to represent and communicate a security-relevant state value that only the server should be authoritative for.

title: Review model exposes client-controlled author field with no server-side derivation contract
description: The Review interface (used as the frontend type for review data, presumably serialized into POST bodies such as /rest/products/:id/reviews or similar review-creation endpoints) defines author as a plain client-settable string field alongside _id and message. Because this type declaration is the contract the frontend code uses to build and send review payloads, it establishes no distinction between fields the client is allowed to set (message) and fields that should be authoritatively derived by the server from the authenticated session (author). If any service constructing a request from this interface allows author to be populated from client-side state (e.g., a locally cached display name) rather than being stripped and re-derived server-side from the JWT/session, an attacker can spoof the displayed author of a review, a trust-boundary violation where the client determines a value the server should independently validate or overwrite. This is a design-level gap in the type itself: it offers no signal (e.g., separate DTO for creation vs. read) that author is untrusted input on write paths, and the same undifferentiated string typing is applied uniformly across all three fields (_id, message, author) with no marker distinguishing server-owned identity/output fields from client-owned input fields. This cannot be fully confirmed without seeing the consuming service/component that populates and POSTs this model, which lies outside this file.

title: Security question model has no encoded strength/verification constraints, reflecting the inherently weak security-question recovery design
description: This file defines the SecurityQuestion data model (id, question text) that underpins the application's security-question based account recovery/verification feature (see related routes POST /api/SecurityQuestions and GET /api/SecurityAnswers in the wider application). The model itself imposes no constraints — there is no encoded notion of answer complexity, uniqueness, rate-limiting metadata, or any structural safeguard against guessable/predictable answers. Knowledge-based security questions (e.g., 'favorite pet', 'favorite pirate') are a well-known weak authentication/recovery factor: answers are frequently guessable, discoverable via OSINT/social engineering, or reused across services. Because the data model that anchors this feature carries no design-level control (e.g., no minimum entropy requirement, no binding to rate-limited verification, no expiration), any component that consumes this model to gate a sensitive action (password reset, identity verification) inherits a workflow that can be defeated by guessing or brute-forcing the answer, since the object shape provides no compensating control. This is a design-level gap rather than an implementation bug: even a bug-free consumer of this interface still permits weak-answer-based bypass, because the model was never designed to carry or enforce answer strength. The entrypoint/consumer code that reads and verifies this model lies outside this file (likely in the security-question REST controller referenced by /api/SecurityQuestions and /api/SecurityAnswers in server.ts), so the concrete exploitation path (e.g., missing rate limiting, case-insensitive/trimmed comparison) cannot be fully confirmed from this file alone.

title: Client-trusted challenge completion/dependency flags used to gate workflow instead of server-side enforcement
description: The Challenge model exposes state fields (`solved`, `tutorialOrder`, `hasTutorial`, `hasSnippet`, `codingChallengeStatus`, `mitigationUrl`, `hasCodingChallenge`, and `ChallengeDependencies[].missing`) that together describe whether a challenge is completed, whether its tutorial/snippet/coding-challenge portions exist and are unlocked, and whether prerequisite challenges are still missing. These are plain client-side TypeScript fields with no accompanying validation or re-derivation logic in this file. If frontend components (outside this file) read this chain of sibling flags in sequence -- checking `solved`, then `tutorialOrder`/`hasTutorial`/`hasSnippet` to decide tutorial gating, then `codingChallengeStatus` together with the required `hasCodingChallenge` flag to decide whether the coding-challenge UI (and the `mitigationUrl` solution hint) should be revealed, and finally `ChallengeDependencies[].missing` to decide whether a dependent challenge can be started -- then every one of these access decisions is being made from data the server merely sent to the client, none of which is re-verified server-side at the point of the sensitive action in this model. An attacker who can directly call the underlying REST endpoints (e.g. the various `/api/Challenges`-style routes visible in the architecture) could invoke actions the UI would otherwise disable based on this whole chain of flags, bypassing the intended multi-step challenge workflow (tutorial/snippet sequencing, coding-challenge unlock, dependency prerequisites) if the server does not independently re-check each condition.

`mitigationUrl` is the reward/solution-adjacent field that a UI may reveal once it believes (from the untrusted `codingChallengeStatus`/`solved` flags) that the challenge or its coding portion is complete -- an example of a sensitive disclosure gated purely by client-held state.

title: Environment-name field (disabledEnv) modeled for client consumption, risking exposure of internal deployment configuration
description: The `disabledEnv` field carries a string presumably identifying the deployment environment(s) in which a challenge is disabled (e.g., 'Docker', 'CTF', a specific hosting name). Because this is defined as part of the client-facing Challenge model -- the same interface object that also carries plainly descriptive fields like `name` and `category` which are clearly meant for display/logging -- `disabledEnv` travels bundled with the rest of the challenge's descriptive data to whatever frontend code renders, filters, or logs a Challenge object. This means environment/deployment details that are otherwise internal implementation concerns are exposed to any client that can fetch challenge data, and can be surfaced or logged incidentally anywhere the object as a whole is handled. This can help an attacker fingerprint the deployment mode or hosting environment and tailor further attacks (e.g., knowing which anti-abuse or CTF-specific protections are active/inactive). This is a design/config choice rather than an implementation bug in this file, and the actual exposure depends on the API endpoint that populates this field (outside this file), so it is reported with reduced confidence.

title: Admin API errors are rethrown without any client-side security logging
description: The getApplicationVersion() method calls the admin-only endpoint '/rest/admin/application-version' and pipes the response through a catchError operator that does nothing but rethrow the original error ('catchError((error: Error) => { throw error })'). No log entry, telemetry event, or monitoring signal is emitted when a call to this privileged admin endpoint fails (e.g., due to an authorization failure, unexpected response, or repeated failed probing). Because this is the only error-handling path for an administrative API call in this service, any abnormal or repeated failure pattern (which could indicate an attacker probing the admin API surface or a misconfigured/broken authorization check) is silently swallowed by the caller with zero observability. While this is client-side code and ultimate authorization is enforced server-side, the complete absence of any logging/telemetry hook here means the frontend contributes nothing to detecting or reconstructing an attack timeline involving misuse of the admin API.

title: Unfiltered request body forwarded to backend on address save/update (mass-assignment enabler)
description: The save() and put() methods accept an opaque `params` object from the caller and forward it verbatim as the HTTP request body to POST/PUT /api/Addresss[/:id], with no field allow-list or stripping of sensitive properties (e.g. ownership/user-id fields, verification flags, or any other model attributes the backend might bind automatically). Both methods build their destination from the single shared `this.host` value (constructed once from environment.hostServer), and neither performs any filtering before concatenating params into the outgoing HTTP call. Because this Angular service is the single choke point between UI forms and the backend API, it is the natural place to enforce which fields are permitted to leave the client, yet it performs no such restriction in either code path. If the calling component (outside this file) ever includes extra properties in the params object (through spread of a fetched object, a shared form model, or a compromised/modified client), those properties are transmitted unchanged to the server on both create and update.

If the backend endpoint returns all address records for the requesting context without enforcing a server-side cap, this single, unparameterized call could pull an unbounded result set into the client (and correspondingly force the server to serialize and transmit an unbounded number of rows), and this file provides no built-in throttling or size bound for repeated calls.

title: Errors from address API calls are rethrown with no security logging
description: Every method in this service (get, getById, save, put, del) uses catchError((err) => { throw err }) (or the typed equivalent), which rethrows the error but never logs it. Failed address operations, including potential authorization failures (e.g. attempting to fetch/update/delete another user's address by ID) or malformed/abusive requests, leave no trace at the point they occur, and this same blind-rethrow pattern repeats identically across every single request method in the class rather than being isolated to one call site. Because this is the shared API client wrapper for all address operations, it is a natural place to record security-relevant failures (401/403 responses, repeated failed lookups by ID suggesting ID enumeration) before propagating them, but no such logging exists anywhere in the file. Whether the error is logged further upstream is outside this file, but within this file there is no correlation ID, no request context, and no log statement of any kind attached to any failure.

title: Unvalidated numeric/path id interpolated directly into request URL
description: getById, put, and del build request URLs via template-literal interpolation of the caller-supplied `id` directly into the path (`${this.host}/${id}`) with no validation that id is a well-formed numeric identifier before use. The same unchecked-interpolation pattern is repeated independently in put() and del(): put() accepts id with no runtime check and interpolates it directly into the PUT URL, and del() only carries a compile-time `number` type annotation (which TypeScript erases at runtime and does not enforce against a caller passing an unexpected value) before interpolating id into the DELETE URL and issuing the request. title: Basket resource identifier trusted from unauthenticated client-side storage (BOLA pattern)
description: The BasketService reads the active basket identifier ('bid') from sessionStorage — a value that lives entirely on the client and can be freely edited via browser devtools or scripting — and uses it verbatim to construct REST calls that fetch and mutate basket contents (e.g. GET /rest/basket/{bid}). The tests confirm this flow: sessionStorage.setItem('bid', '42') at line 122 is picked up by updateNumberOfCartItems() and directly becomes the path parameter in the outgoing request at line 127. The surrounding setup shows the full path the value travels: localStorage token is set first so the service takes the authenticated (non-guest) branch that trusts the bid value (line 121), a totals array and subscription are established to observe the eventual result (lines 123-124), updateNumberOfCartItems() is invoked and internally reads the untrusted bid to build the request (line 126), the request is matched and its response supplies basket/product data (lines 129-136) which is then reduced into the emitted total (line 137) — all without any point in this path verifying that basket 42 belongs to the current session/user. If the real service and API mirror this test behavior, an authenticated user who edits their own sessionStorage 'bid' value to another user's numeric basket id would have that basket fetched/updated using the arbitrary id, which is the classic BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) pattern: the object identifier is fully attacker-controlled and used directly in a lookup with no ownership check visible anywhere in this flow.

title: Caller-supplied basketId embedded unchecked into BasketItems create/update bodies (mass assignment / cross-basket write)
description: mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket(basketId) takes a numeric basket identifier directly as a parameter and uses it both to look up the target basket (GET /rest/basket/{basketId}) and — critically — to populate the BasketId field of new BasketItem creation requests (POST /api/BasketItems/ with body { ProductId: 2, BasketId: 42, quantity: 3 } at line 228) as well as to select which existing item to PUT-update (PUT /api/BasketItems/100 at line 221). The full path shows the attacker-controlled guest-basket contents (set in sessionStorage at line 201, entirely client-editable) flowing through: the merge call is made with a caller-supplied basketId (line 208), the existing basket contents for that id are fetched (line 212) and its response supplies an existing item and quantity (line 213) which is combined with the guest quantity to compute a new value; the resulting PUT (line 221) explicitly sends quantity:7 (line 222-223) targeting an item that lives under the caller-chosen basket, and even when that write fails (line 224, simulated 500, swallowed as 'best effort') the flow proceeds to create a brand-new BasketItem via POST (line 226-227) whose body directly embeds BasketId:42 (line 228) taken from the caller-supplied parameter. title: Client-controlled basket identifier used for all basket operations without ownership verification (BOLA-enabling design)
description: BasketService exposes get/put/del/checkout/applyCoupon/find methods that take an arbitrary numeric `id` and issue HTTP requests to `/api/BasketItems/:id` or `/rest/basket/:id` with no check that the identifier belongs to the currently authenticated user. The basket id consumed by updateNumberOfCartItems() is read directly from sessionStorage ('bid'), a value that lives in the browser and can be modified by the user via devtools or scripting. Nothing in this file derives the id from a trusted server-issued session claim, nor does it perform any ownership check before dispatching get/put/del/checkout calls. Because the object-level authorization decision is pushed entirely to whatever service consumes these calls, if the backend endpoint (outside this file) does not itself re-validate basket ownership per request, a user can substitute another user's basket id here and the client will happily submit get/update/delete/checkout requests for it. This is the classic BOLA pattern from the client side: the resource identifier is caller/browser controlled and no per-resource ownership gate exists in the code that assembles and sends the request.

title: mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket accepts an unverified target basket id and merges/writes items into it
description: mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket(targetBasketId) is a public method whose targetBasketId is supplied entirely by its caller (outside this file). The function immediately reduces the local guest basket into a per-product quantity map, then (if non-empty) uses targetBasketId to fetch a basket via find(), builds a map of that basket's existing products, and for each merged guest item either PUTs an updated quantity onto an existing BasketItem or POSTs a new BasketItem tied to targetBasketId via save(). There is no check anywhere in this file confirming that targetBasketId is the basket owned by the currently authenticated user before any of these reads or writes occur. If the caller can be tricked into supplying a different basket id — or if that id is itself derived from tamperable client state — this function will silently merge and persist guest-cart data into an arbitrary basket via multiple write requests, amplifying the BOLA risk described in the ownership finding above into an actual state-changing merge operation, after which the local guest basket is cleared as if the merge legitimately succeeded.

title: Unencoded interpolation of user-supplied coupon and basket id into request URL path
description: applyCoupon(id, coupon) builds the request URL by directly interpolating the `coupon` string (and `id`) into a template literal used as the HTTP PUT target: `${this.hostServer}/rest/basket/${id}/coupon/${coupon}`. Neither value is URI-encoded before being embedded into the URL path segment. The same pattern (unencoded id in the path) appears in find(), get(), put(), del(), checkout(). Because coupon is attacker/user-controlled free text (coupon codes entered by the user), a value containing path-manipulating characters (e.g. `../`, `%2e%2e/`, extra slashes) is inserted verbatim into the outbound request path, letting the constructed request path diverge from the intended `/rest/basket/:id/coupon/:coupon` route and instead target a different path on the same host than the developer intended. This is a URL/path-injection defect: user input reaches a code-interpreting sink (the HTTP client's URL parser/router) without validation or encoding.

title: Captcha fetch errors are swallowed without any security logging
description: The getCaptcha() method wraps the HTTP GET to the captcha endpoint in an RxJS catchError operator that does nothing but re-throw the original error (`catchError((err) => { throw err })`). While server-side logging may exist elsewhere, this file — the sole place client-side captcha errors are observed — discards the error context instead of recording it, which removes a potential signal used to detect automated abuse of the captcha-protected flow.

title: Continue-code recovery token transmitted and asserted as a URL path segment
description: The tests confirm that ChallengeService.restoreProgress()/restoreProgressFindIt()/restoreProgressFixIt() build requests where the caller-supplied continue code (a sensitive, single-use style recovery/progress-restoration secret) is embedded directly in the URL path, e.g. 'http://localhost:3000/rest/continue-code/apply/CODE'. This is the confirmed, real request shape the client emits (the spec asserts the exact URL and PUT method, and completes the round-trip via req.flush), meaning this is the actual wire contract used by the application, not just a test artifact. Placing a bearer-style secret in the URL path is a known anti-pattern: URLs are routinely recorded in web server access logs, reverse proxy logs, browser history, and can leak via Referer headers to third-party resources loaded on the same page. The same construction is repeated verbatim for the 'Find It' continue-code variant, showing the pattern is systemic across the service rather than a one-off. Anyone with access to those logs (ops staff, a compromised proxy, shared/public terminals) can capture and replay a user's continue code to restore/hijack their challenge progress.

This is a design-level question — whether the server re-derives ownership of the code rather than trusting the client-presented value — that cannot be fully confirmed from this spec file since the server implementation and any auth interceptors are outside this file's scope.

title: Unhandled JSON.parse exception can permanently hang the chat streaming generator
description: The SSE-style stream handler parses each 'data: ' line with JSON.parse(data) at line 59 with no surrounding try/catch. If the backend (or an attacker positioned to influence the LLM's raw output, e.g. via a successful prompt-injection that causes the model to emit a line beginning with 'data: ' followed by non-JSON text, or any malformed/truncated chunk boundary) produces a line that is not valid JSON, JSON.parse throws synchronously inside the RxJS `next` handler. This exception is not caught anywhere in this file: `done` is never set to true, `resolve()` is never invoked for that terminal state, and the observable's `error`/`complete` callbacks may not fire for a synchronous throw inside `next` depending on RxJS version/behavior. Because the async generator's while loop at lines 96-102 awaits a Promise that only resolves when `resolve()` is called, a thrown exception that bypasses the intended resolve/done-setting paths leaves the generator suspended forever on `await new Promise<void>((r) => { resolve = r })`. This causes an indefinite hang of that chat session (denial of service for the caller) and leaks the pending subscription/promise, since the design never wraps the parsing step in error handling to guarantee `done`/`resolve` are always eventually triggered.

title: Model-generated tool calls are forwarded verbatim without validation, enabling excessive agency downstream
description: The service extracts `delta.tool_calls` directly from the parsed LLM response (line 74) and passes the raw structure (function name and arguments string) through the ChatChunk stream to the caller with zero validation, allow-listing, or sanitization of the function name or arguments. This file performs no verification that the requested tool/function is one the current user is authorized to invoke, nor does it bound the number or size of tool calls per turn. If the downstream consumer (outside this file) executes tool calls based on trust in this data without independently re-checking authorization, an attacker who can influence the conversation (directly, or indirectly through injected content the model reads) gains the ability to trigger privileged actions the model was never meant to grant unilaterally.

title: Unvalidated LLM tool_call directives passed through to caller without verification
description: The spec exercises ChatService.streamMessages() and confirms that when the backend (which proxies an LLM completion stream) emits a tool_calls delta, the service surfaces the tool call's function name and raw arguments string directly to the consumer (deltaToolCalls) with no test coverage of any validation, allow-listing, or argument schema check performed before exposing it. Tracing the full path: the test messages enter the service call, the returned generator is drained into an accumulator by an unfiltered for-await loop that pushes every chunk (including tool-call chunks) verbatim, the mocked HTTP response delivers the raw tool_calls payload, and after the request completes the test asserts that the function name and (by extension) the raw arguments are exposed unchanged. At no point in this path is there a step that inspects, allow-lists, or strips the tool call before it reaches whatever downstream code consumes the generator (e.g. a chat component that executes the named tool). This establishes that the model's output is trusted verbatim as an instruction to be acted upon. If the downstream consumer executes tool calls based solely on this unvalidated data (name/arguments controlled by the model, which in turn can be influenced by attacker-supplied conversation content), this is a textbook LLM06 Excessive Agency pattern. The actual execution sink lives outside this file, so full exploitability cannot be confirmed here, but the interface tested provides no verification hook anywhere along the path.

title: No evidence of input sanitization/fencing on user message content sent to LLM backend
description: Across all tests, the messages array sent to streamMessages (e.g. { role: 'user', content: 'hello' }) is passed straight through as the POST body to /rest/chat with no test asserting any escaping, delimiting, or moderation of the content field. Tracing the full path: the raw user content is defined, handed unmodified into streamMessages, the generator is drained by an accumulation loop, the outbound POST request is captured by the mock, and the only assertion made against that request checks the HTTP method — never the body content — before the request is flushed to completion and accepted as valid. This is consistent with a design where user-supplied conversation content is forwarded to the LLM backend without any fencing that would prevent it from being interpreted as system-level instructions once concatenated into a prompt (a prerequisite condition for LLM01 prompt injection). This cannot be fully confirmed from the spec alone since the actual prompt-construction logic lives in chat.service.ts, not in this file, but the tested contract provides no indication such protection exists anywhere along the traced path.

title: Code snippet retrieval tested without any authentication/authorization context, suggesting endpoint may lack access control
description: The spec exercises CodeSnippetService.get() against the real backend route '/snippets/:challengeId' but never sets, mocks, or asserts on any Authorization header, bearer token, or session credential in the HTTP request that httpMock.expectOne intercepts. The test module configuration (line 16) wires up only the plain HttpClient/HttpClientTesting providers and the service itself — no auth or bearer-token interceptor is registered or exercised anywhere in the suite, so the path from service instantiation through the call to the mocked response never involves an identity check. Neither the happy-path test (lines 26-39) nor the error-path test (lines 41-52) verify that the service attaches an auth token or that unauthenticated/unauthorized requests are rejected differently from a plain 404. If the underlying service and its server-side route indeed omit any identity check (which cannot be fully confirmed from this file alone, since the service implementation lives elsewhere), any client could retrieve arbitrary challenge code snippets — including snippets tied to challenges not yet unlocked or exposed to the current user — by supplying any challenge identifier. Because this spec is the only visible evidence of how the service is expected to behave, and it encodes no expectation of an auth check on this data-retrieval path, it points to a design that treats snippet retrieval as unauthenticated by default. This is a weak/absent-check finding on a trust boundary (client-supplied challenge id fully determines server response) rather than a confirmed exploit, hence lower confidence.

title: Continue-code progress restoration trusts client-supplied code as sole authorization
description: restoreProgress, restoreProgressFindIt and restoreProgressFixIt take an arbitrary continueCode string from the caller and PUT it directly to the backend's apply endpoint with no ownership check performed anywhere in this file (and none of these functions verify that the continueCode belongs to the current session/user before submitting it). The design treats mere possession of a continue-code string as sufficient authorization to overwrite the current user's challenge-solve progress. If continue codes are guessable, leaked, or brute-forced (they are a deterministic encoding of solved-challenge state, a known weakness in this class of feature), any user who obtains or guesses another user's code can restore that state into their own account via this client, without the server (as invoked from here) ever confirming the caller is the rightful owner of that progress. The entrypoint (the component that collects the continueCode from user input, e.g. a paste field) lies outside this file; this file is the boundary where the untrusted string is accepted and forwarded to a state-changing endpoint. The same unchecked pattern is repeated identically for all three progress namespaces (main, findIt, fixIt), showing the design gap is structural rather than a one-off omission.

title: No throttling on repeated continue-code guesses enabling brute-force enumeration
description: The restoreProgress family of methods issues a PUT request for any continueCode string supplied by the caller, with no rate limiting, backoff, or attempt-count control visible anywhere in this service. Since continue codes are a compact deterministic encoding, an attacker can script rapid, repeated calls through this client (or directly against the underlying endpoint it wraps) to brute-force valid codes belonging to other accounts. Nothing in this file bounds the number or frequency of such attempts across any of the three parallel endpoints, so the cost of large-scale guessing falls entirely on the backend with no client-side or observable server-side safeguard represented here.

title: Failed/invalid continue-code restore attempts are not logged for security monitoring
description: Every network call in this service funnels errors through catchError((err) => { throw err }), which simply rethrows the error without recording any detail (timestamp, attempted code, requester context) anywhere in this file. For the security-sensitive continue-code apply operations in particular, a failed attempt is indistinguishable from a benign network error at the point where security monitoring would need to detect a pattern of repeated invalid-code submissions (a hallmark of brute-force enumeration). No correlation ID, attempt count, or log emission exists in this client layer to support reconstructing an attack timeline for these state-changing calls, and the same silent-rethrow pattern recurs across all three continue-code variants.

title: No transport-security enforcement on backend host used for state-changing and credentialed requests
description: All requests in this service are built from this.hostServer (derived from environment.hostServer) with no check or enforcement in this file that the configured host uses HTTPS before dispatching requests, including state-changing PUT calls that carry continue codes. If the environment configuration defaults to or is misconfigured with a plain http:// origin (a value not visible from this file), continue codes and other data sent through this service would traverse the network without transport confidentiality, and this file contains no defensive check to catch that misconfiguration before making the call.

title: Unbounded, unthrottled challenge-verification requests allow brute-forcing the correct fix
description: The check() method posts an attacker/user-controlled `selectedFix` index (and `key`) to the backend verification endpoint with no client-side attempt limiting, delay, or lockout. Because the 'correct answer' space for this kind of code-fix challenge is small (a handful of candidate fixes returned by get()), a caller can script repeated calls to check() cycling through every possible `selectedFix` value until the server returns verdict:true, defeating the intended purpose of the challenge (the user must reason about the correct fix) via brute-force guessing rather than legitimate use. Nothing in this file rate-limits, debounces, or caps the number of verification attempts, and each call triggers a network round trip and presumably server-side computation, which also enables resource-consumption abuse via automated rapid-fire requests. This is a design gap: the server-trust model assumes a human trying fixes occasionally, but the client interface offers no compensating control for automated exhaustive guessing.

title: Errors from snippet retrieval are rethrown without any logging
description: The get() method's RxJS pipeline uses catchError((err) => { throw err }) to handle failures from the HTTP GET request to the /snippets/{key} endpoint. title: Unvalidated/unencoded key interpolated directly into request URL
description: The get() method builds the request URL by directly template-interpolating the caller-supplied 'key' parameter into a path segment (`${this.host}/${key}`) with no validation, allow-listing, or URI encoding (e.g. encodeURIComponent). Because the server is expected to be the authority that decides which snippet a given key maps to, but the client performs no sanity checking on the value before sending it, any component that forwards route parameters or other externally influenced strings into this service can cause requests to arbitrary path segments beneath /snippets (e.g. path traversal-like segments such as '../' or unexpected values) with no client-side guard. title: Test confirms ComplaintService.save() forwards arbitrary caller-supplied object fields to the Complaints API without any allow-list
description: The spec file demonstrates that ComplaintService.save() accepts an arbitrary JavaScript object (here `{ foo: 'bar' }`) and passes it, unmodified, as the POST body to `/api/Complaints/`. There is no evidence in this test suite that the service restricts, validates, or allow-lists which properties of the object are sent to the backend. If the underlying Complaint model has sensitive or privileged fields (e.g., an id, a user reference, or a status/verification flag), a caller of this service could set those properties simply by including them in the object passed to `save()`, and they would be forwarded as-is to the REST endpoint. The actual enforcement (or lack thereof) lives in complaint.service.ts and ultimately the server-side Complaints handler, both outside this file, but this spec is the clearest evidence available here that the client-side service imposes no allow-list on the object it serializes into the request body. Tracing the full test path: the service and mock harness are obtained (lines 41-42), an error-capture variable is set up (line 44) before the arbitrary-body call is made (line 45); the mock then intercepts the exact outgoing request without any assertion that its body was filtered or restricted (line 46), and the test completes the exchange by flushing a synthetic error response, at no point checking or constraining which properties of the original object reached the request body (line 47), while the final assertions only verify the HTTP error status, not the shape of the transmitted payload (lines 48-49).

title: Configuration fetch failures are silently propagated without security logging
description: The getApplicationConfiguration() method requests the application configuration from the backend and wires a catchError operator that does nothing but re-throw the original error (line 121: `catchError((err) => { throw err })`). No log entry, telemetry event, or monitoring hook records that the configuration fetch failed, why it failed, or which client/session encountered it. Because this is the mechanism the entire SPA depends on for feature flags, security-relevant toggles (e.g. challenges.safetyMode, hackingInstructor.isEnabled, ctf.systemWideNotifications.url) and OAuth client configuration, repeated or anomalous failures here (e.g. an attacker tampering with the admin endpoint, a MITM injecting malformed responses, or a denial-of-service against the config endpoint) leave no trace for detection or incident reconstruction. An operator investigating a security incident involving unexpected application behavior would find no log evidence that configuration retrieval was failing or being manipulated.

title: Application-wide configuration served from an '/rest/admin' path without visible authorization enforcement in the client
description: The service builds its request host as `this.hostServer + '/rest/admin'` (line 114) and fetches essential, app-wide configuration data (feature flags, challenge settings, OAuth client id/redirects, CTF notification URL) from what is nominally an administrative API namespace (line 121: GET '/rest/admin/application-configuration'). No authentication token, admin-role check, or authorization header is attached in this file before issuing the request, and the response is trusted and cached indefinitely in `configObservable` for reuse by the whole application (lines 115-123) without any integrity or origin validation. If the backend does not itself gate this specific route behind an authorization check (a design assumption this file cannot verify but which the URL naming implies should exist), any unauthenticated caller — not just admins — can read and, depending on backend enforcement, an attacker with access to modify this endpoint's backing data could poison configuration values (e.g. safetyMode, redirect URLs, notification URLs) consumed trustingly by every client in the application, since the client performs no verification that the returned config originates from a legitimate, unmodified source.

title: Unvalidated arbitrary payload forwarded directly to Complaints API (mass-assignment surface)
description: The `save()` method accepts a parameter typed as `any` and forwards it verbatim as the JSON body of a POST to `/api/Complaints/`. There is no shape validation, field allow-listing, or sanitisation performed in this service before the object reaches the network call. Any caller in the application (or any code able to invoke this service, e.g. via a compromised component or a manipulated form binding) can attach arbitrary extra fields to the complaint object — for example ownership/user identifiers, verification flags, or other properties the server-side model may blindly trust (a classic mass-assignment pattern). Because this file establishes no contract on what `params` may contain, the design never re-derives or bounds the data before it leaves the client, pushing 100% of the trust decision onto the server. The HTTP client and target URL used to carry that unvalidated object are wired up at construction time (injecting HttpClient and building the host string from environment configuration) and then reused unchanged as the transport for the unvalidated body. If the server-side Complaints handler is equally permissive (which this file cannot see, but which the design here does nothing to prevent), an attacker can inject fields the business logic never intended the client to control.

The request that generates these errors is built from the injected HttpClient and the environment-derived host before being dispatched, and the response is piped through map() before catchError() discards the error context; server-side logging is outside this file, but this file is the last point at which the outbound request/response pair is fully known on the client, and it discards that information instead of recording it for monitoring/debugging.

description: save(params: any) forwards whatever object it is given straight into an HTTP POST with no size cap, no chunking, and no throttling applied at this layer. Juice Shop's complaint feature is known to allow attaching file content (e.g., base64-encoded uploads) inside the complaint payload; because this service applies no bound to the size of `params` and no client-side rate limiting, a caller (or a compromised/scripted client bypassing the UI and calling this service or its underlying endpoint directly) can repeatedly submit very large bodies against the fixed endpoint assembled from environment configuration. title: Test suite mocks CountryMappingService against a plaintext HTTP endpoint
description: The spec file exercises CountryMappingService.getCountryMapping() and mocks the network call to 'http://localhost:3000/rest/country-mapping' (lines 33 and 49). Because HttpTestingController.expectOne() matches the exact URL the service under test issues its request to, this indicates the CountryMappingService itself is configured to call the REST API over plain HTTP rather than HTTPS. If this base URL construction (protocol + host) is not overridden per-environment in production builds, sensitive data returned by /rest/country-mapping (or other endpoints built the same way) would be transmitted without transport-layer encryption, exposing responses to network-level interception/tampering. This is inferred indirectly from the test fixture rather than directly observed in a config file, since the actual URL-building logic lives in country-mapping.service.ts, which is outside this file. Tracing through both test cases in this file shows the same insecure endpoint is exercised twice, in two independent test setups, confirming the pattern is a consistent property of the service rather than a one-off artifact of a single test.

title: Failed GDPR erasure and data-export requests are silently rethrown without any logging
description: erase(params: any) accepts an untyped, arbitrary object from its caller and forwards it verbatim as the body of a POST to /rest/user/erasure-request — an operation that deletes/erases user data and is inherently irreversible. title: Caller-controlled arbitrary URL passed directly to HttpClient without validation (SSRF-like / token-exfiltration design flaw)
description: The `fetchNotification` method takes a fully caller-supplied `url` string and passes it verbatim into `this.http.get<...>(url)` with no validation, allow-listing, or restriction to a known/trusted backend endpoint (e.g. the app's own `/rest/...` API). A component such as `CtfSystemWideNotificationService` should almost certainly only ever fetch the system-wide notification from a single, fixed, internal API path. Instead, the design allows the caller (and, transitively, whatever upstream data — route parameter, query string, stored config, or user input — feeds that caller) to redirect the underlying HTTP request to an arbitrary origin. Angular applications commonly configure an `HttpInterceptor` that automatically attaches the user's Authorization/Bearer token or session cookie to every outgoing `HttpClient` request regardless of destination host. If such an interceptor exists in this app (a very common Juice-Shop-style pattern), an attacker who can influence the `url` value reaching this service can cause the victim's browser to send its authentication token to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in session/token theft. Even without an interceptor, this is a textbook 'trust assumption violation': the service trusts the caller to supply a safe destination rather than deriving/hardcoding it itself, which is exactly the kind of design gap that lets an attacker turn a benign 'fetch a banner message' feature into a data-exfiltration or open-proxy primitive. The `this.http` instance used to perform the call (line 20) is a generic, un-scoped `HttpClient` injected with no base-URL restriction or request-guard visible in this file, so nothing between the parameter and the network call constrains the destination. The vulnerability is structural — no implementation-level input check would fix it without redesigning the service to accept, at most, an identifier that is resolved server-side/internally to a fixed URL.

title: Conversation history stored in a globally-keyed, unscoped localStorage bucket (no per-user isolation)
description: The ConversationStorageService under test persists all chat conversations under a single fixed localStorage key (STORAGE_KEY = 'juiceshop_chat_conversations') with no reference to the currently authenticated user or session. title: Backup restore path trusts unsigned, attacker-authored file content to overwrite security-relevant challenge/progress state
description: The spec exercises LocalBackupService.restore(), which is fed a raw File object whose entire content is an attacker-controlled JSON string (line 75). The only integrity check the tests exercise is a bare numeric 'version' field (line 83: version 0 is rejected, version 1 is accepted at line 75) — there is no signature, checksum, HMAC, or any cryptographic proof that the JSON originated from a legitimate export produced by this same application. Once the version check passes, arbitrary fields from the file (e.g. 'language', and by the symmetry of save()/restore() shown in the later test, continueCode / continueCodeFindIt / continueCodeFixIt) are written straight into the cookie store, which the rest of the app (ChallengeService) treats as authoritative fallback state for whether challenges have been solved. Lines 93-95 show the exact cookie keys (continueCode, continueCodeFindIt, continueCodeFixIt) being seeded, lines 98-100 show the server-side source of truth for those codes being made unavailable, and line 104/106 show save() proceeding to use those locally-held (and, via restore(), locally-forgeable) cookie values as the trusted fallback with only a diagnostic log and no re-validation. title: Unauthenticated enumeration of user security questions by email, with no logging or throttling
description: findBy(email) sends an unauthenticated GET request to the backend's security-question lookup endpoint using only a caller-supplied email address, and returns the associated security question text directly to the caller (response.question). title: Order tracking endpoint has no client-side ownership/ownership-token enforcement, enabling order ID enumeration (IDOR by design)
description: The find method accepts an arbitrary string params from its caller, URL-encodes it, and issues a GET request to /rest/track-order/{params} with no additional binding to the requesting user's identity, session, or an unguessable/opaque order token. Because the authorization decision (if any) happens entirely server-side and is invisible from this file, the client offers no compensating control (e.g. requiring a per-order secret/token alongside the ID) for what is otherwise a mass-enumerable primary key lookup exposed directly to the caller.

title: No authentication credentials attached to Socket.IO connection
description: The service opens the Socket.IO connection (both branches at lines 22-24 and line 26) without attaching any authentication token, session identifier, or user credential to the `io()` call (e.g., via the `auth` option or a query parameter). Socket.IO's own auth mechanism (`io(url, { auth: {...} })`) is available but unused. As a result, any code path that relies on this socket for real-time features (chat, notifications, order updates, etc.) has no way for the server to bind socket events to an authenticated identity unless the server independently re-validates every incoming event payload. If the corresponding server-side handlers trust the socket connection implicitly (a common pattern paired with an unauthenticated client socket like this), any anonymous client can open a connection and send/receive events meant for authenticated users, because the client never establishes who it is at the transport layer. This is a design gap: the file establishes the trust boundary (the socket channel) without ever deciding to authenticate it, leaving that decision entirely — and silently — to whatever server code happens to be reached. Tracing the full construction path confirms neither branch (the same-origin branch nor the external-hostServer branch) ever supplies credentials, so the gap is structural, not an omission on one code path only.

description: The spec asserts that VulnLinesService.check() posts to the absolute, hardcoded URL 'http://localhost:3000/snippets/verdict' rather than a relative API path or an environment-driven base URL. This confirms the underlying service (vuln-lines.service.ts, not shown here) hardcodes a development-only host/port. If this hardcoded value ships to production builds (or is not properly overridden per-environment), it can cause the app to send challenge-verification requests to the wrong/unreachable host, silently fail security-relevant functionality, or — if an attacker controls a local listener on port 3000 in a shared/dev environment — allow interception or spoofing of verdict responses. This is a configuration-management defect: connection endpoints should be sourced from environment configuration, not hardcoded literals baked into the client bundle. The same literal URL is exercised and confirmed a second time in the error-handling test, showing it is a fixed value used consistently across all call paths rather than a one-off test artifact.

title: No verification that failed challenge-verification requests are logged or monitored
description: The error-handling test (lines 34-44) simulates a failed request to the snippets/verdict endpoint (a security-relevant operation — verification of a submitted coding-challenge 'fix') and only asserts that the HTTP status code is propagated to the caller. There is no assertion, mock, or expectation involving any logging/monitoring call (e.g., a logging service, analytics, or audit trail) being invoked on failure. Walking the full error path — service/httpMock setup, error variable declaration, the failing call, the mocked network error, and the final assertion — shows every step deals only with propagating the raw HTTP error to the subscriber; at no point is a security-relevant logging or alerting side-effect exercised or verified for this failure, even though repeated failed verdict submissions could indicate an attacker probing/brute-forcing challenge answers.
